tldr: We developed "UMI-Live," an open-source system that collects bimanual manipulation data effortlessly using handheld grippers integrating LiDAR, cameras, and onboard compute without any external tracking or per-environment calibration, immediately turning recordings into datasets in the background for real-robot learning.
hero_caption: The exterior appearance of the UMI-Live handheld device and a bimanual manipulation session. Demonstrations of bimanual tasks can be smoothly recorded in unconstrained, in-the-wild environments without physical robots, free from external cameras or tripods.
overview:
In imitation learning for robot manipulation, high-quality human demonstration data collected across diverse environments is key to boosting performance. However, conventional teleoperation requires transporting physical robots and safety infrastructure, creating a major obstacle to scaling up collection sites. To address this, the Universal Manipulation Interface (UMI) emerged, allowing humans to demonstrate tasks using handheld grippers. Yet existing approaches still suffered from practical operational hurdles, such as requiring backpack PCs or stationary external trackers, as well as manual effort for post-hoc SLAM processing and data formatting.

To solve this, the authors propose "UMI-Live," a completely self-contained bimanual collection system that eliminates the need for external tracking and per-environment calibration. Each handheld gripper integrates LiDAR, an IMU, an ultra-wide camera, a Raspberry Pi, and a swappable battery, allowing synchronized bimanual recording with the press of a single button. Furthermore, as soon as recording finishes, an asynchronous pipeline runs parallel SLAM reconstruction on a server and automatically generates datasets in the LeRobot robotics library format, enabling operators to collect demonstrations continuously without waiting for processing.

As an empirical validation, the authors fine-tuned state-of-the-art Vision-Language-Action (VLA) models, $\pi_{0.5}$ and MolmoAct2, using approximately 40 hours of bimanual demonstration data collected across different locations and lighting conditions. On a real dual-arm robot (YAM) orange pick-and-place task, the models achieved high success rates of 10/10 with $\pi_{0.5}$ and 8/10 with MolmoAct2, proving that handheld collection data is extremely effective for real-robot policy training.
contributions: Designed and released reproducible bimanual data collection hardware that integrates sensors, onboard compute, and power locally, eliminating external trackers and per-environment calibration.

Built an end-to-end automated processing pipeline that runs parallel SLAM and gripper width estimation in the background immediately upon recording completion, instantly publishing datasets in LeRobot format.
Fully open-sourced a dual-arm YAM robot teleoperation system, VLA model training and inference pipelines, and an approximately 40-hour bimanual manipulation dataset.
Demonstrated that training predominantly on in-the-wild UMI data enables state-of-the-art VLA models such as $\pi_{0.5}$ and MolmoAct2 to operate with high accuracy on physical robots.

sections.heading: Collecting bimanual demonstration data effortlessly even without a robot
sections.summary: Robot imitation learning requires large, diverse demonstration datasets, but transporting physical robots everywhere is extremely difficult. We explain the motivation behind UMI-Live, which evolves the handheld UMI approach by eliminating external gear and automating processing.
sections.details:
Advances in imitation learning have enabled robots to acquire complex tasks like folding towels and picking objects. In recent years, Vision-Language-Action (VLA) models such as $\pi_{0.5}$ and World Action Models (WAMs) have attracted significant attention, but adapting them to new environments still requires high-quality demonstration data with action labels.

However, teleoperating physical robots as in DROID or ABC-130K requires setting up the robot, power sources, and safety enclosures on site every time, limiting scalability. To address this, UMI (Universal Manipulation Interface) emerged, enabling humans to demonstrate tasks directly using handheld grippers without physical robots.

Yet conventional UMI systems remained cumbersome to operate. They required carrying backpack PCs, using external optical trackers, or manually running SLAM (Simultaneous Localization and Mapping) and reformatting datasets after recording. This was the biggest bottleneck. UMI-Live removes these hassles, offering a workflow where operators simply press a single button to collect data continuously while training-ready datasets are automatically constructed behind the scenes.

sections.heading: Evolution and context: from robot teleoperation to handheld devices
sections.summary: We review the progress from real-robot teleoperation to handheld interfaces like the original UMI and FastUMI, clarifying how UMI-Live achieves both self-contained hardware and automated software.
sections.details:
### Robot Teleoperation Data Collection
Teleoperating physical robots (e.g., ALOHA, DROID) provides data that matches the kinematics and dynamics of the robot directly, but it tends to lock data collection into fixed environments. UMI-Live primarily adopts a handheld system for collecting in-the-wild demonstrations without a robot, while also offering a teleoperation setup to fine-tune quirks of the target physical robot, combining the strengths of both approaches.

### Lineage of Handheld UMI Systems
The original UMI achieved portable demonstrations using wrist cameras and GoPro visual-inertial tracking. Subsequently, LiDAR-based UMI-3D, ActiveUMI combining VR goggles with backpack PCs, and HiFi-UMI using head-mounted stereo cameras were proposed. However, many of these setups involved external stationary rigs or heavy backpacks, constraining mobility. UMI-Live mounts LiDAR, IMU, compute, and power entirely onto each standalone gripper, enabling truly cordless, unconstrained bimanual data collection.

### Learning Software and Ecosystem
To smoothly bridge collected data to policy training, integration with open-source standards like LeRobot is underway. UMI-Live establishes a reproducible pipeline providing end-to-end support for asynchronous data transfer, parallel SLAM processing, automatic publishing in LeRobot format, and policy inference on a dual-arm YAM robot.

sections.heading: From hardware to automated processing: UMI-Live system architecture
sections.summary: We detail the lightweight, self-contained bimanual gripper hardware and the parallel data processing pipeline that runs automatically in the background at the push of a button, freeing operators from manual data conversion.
sections.details:
### 3.1 Hardware Design
Each UMI-Live gripper integrates a compact LiDAR with a built-in IMU (RoboSense Airy), an ultra-wide global shutter USB camera (800x600 resolution at 30 fps), a Raspberry Pi 5, and a swappable battery module (weighing 1.42 kg per unit). Because no overhead cameras are used, the hand-mounted ultra-wide camera is designed to capture both the workspace and surrounding context.

The gripper mechanism has also been refined. Bearings are used on the trigger and sector gear pivots to reduce backlash, realizing smooth parallel opening and closing. The fingertips consist of a rigid PLA+ base and a thin TPU (thermoplastic polyurethane) contact layer, balancing the ability to securely pinch tiny parts like screws while conforming flexibly to object shapes. Gripper finger opening width is accurately measured by reading an ArUco marker (a square fiducial marker) placed on the finger mount with the camera.

### 3.2 Operator Workflow and Recording
Operation is simple. A single button press on one gripper simultaneously starts and stops recording on both handheld devices. A small rear-mounted LCD screen displays recording status and transfer progress to the server, so operators do not need to walk back to check a PC screen.

### 3.3 Automated Data Processing Pipeline
Once recorded data is sent to the server over local Wi-Fi, the following steps run fully automatically and in parallel:
- **Precise Time Synchronization**: Using Chrony (network time synchronization) and gPTP (Precision Time Protocol), timestamps across the Pis and LiDARs are synchronized within 5 ms.
- **Trajectory Estimation (SLAM) and Finger Width Measurement**: The GLIM algorithm independently estimates poses from each hand's LiDAR and IMU data to compute Tool Center Point (TCP) trajectories. Gripper width is calculated from the geometry of the ArUco tag into a normalized value (0 to 1).
- **Dataset Aggregation**: Trajectories are converted to relative poses with the episode start pose as the origin, automatically saved in LeRobot format, and optionally uploaded directly to Hugging Face.

### 3.4 Policy Learning and Deployment
Model inputs are restricted to left and right wrist camera images, the current gripper opening degree, and natural language task instructions; robot-specific joint angles and absolute coordinates are excluded. This minimizes the representational gap between human handheld demonstrations and physical robot data.

sections.heading: Real-robot evaluation: how well does a policy work using UMI data from a different environment?
sections.summary: We evaluated performance on a bimanual task of placing six oranges on a table into a bowl. Even when trained predominantly on handheld data collected in an entirely different room and lighting condition, $\pi_{0.5}$ achieved a 100% task success rate.
sections.details:
### 4.1 Experimental Setup
The evaluation task requires picking six oranges randomly placed on a table using both arms (i2RT YAM arms) and transferring them into a bowl. The task is judged a success once all six oranges are in the bowl, and a failure if any are dropped or left outside (re-grasping and recovering dropped oranges are allowed).

An important experimental condition is that **the handheld UMI-Live demonstration data was collected in a completely different room under different lighting conditions from the real-robot evaluation site**. Only a small number of teleoperation demonstrations were collected in the target environment.

### 4.2 Training Conditions and Baselines
A mixture of 296 collected UMI episodes and 75 real teleoperation episodes was used. The latest VLA models, $\pi_{0.5}$ and MolmoAct2, were fine-tuned across different data mixture ratios:
- $\pi_{0.5}$: 95% UMI / 5% teleoperation, and 90% UMI / 10% teleoperation
- MolmoAct2: 75% UMI / 25% teleoperation
- Baseline: The official pretrained MolmoAct2 checkpoint without additional fine-tuning

### 4.3 Results and Analysis
Across 10 evaluation trials, the models achieved remarkable results:
- **$\pi_{0.5}$ (90/10 mix)**: Achieved a complete task success rate of **10/10 (100%)**. Even with a 95/5 mix, it demonstrated very high performance at 9/10.
- **MolmoAct2 (75/25 mix)**: Succeeded in **8/10 trials (80%)**. In contrast, the official checkpoint without fine-tuning failed completely at 0/10 (0% success rate).

These results clearly demonstrate that even when the vast majority of data (75–95%) consists of human handheld demonstrations gathered in a separate room without robots, mixing in a small amount of target robot data enables learning highly accurate bimanual coordination policies.

captions.F7: Autonomous rollouts during real-robot evaluation viewed from the wrist cameras. Within the field of view of the ultra-wide cameras, both arms sequentially pick up oranges and place them accurately into the bowl.

sections.heading: Releasing a large-scale open dataset of approximately 40 hours
sections.summary: We released roughly 40 hours (3,255 episodes) of bimanual manipulation data across three tasks: orange placement, water pouring, and towel folding. All data is available on Hugging Face in a LeRobot-compatible format.
sections.details:
As a contribution to the research community, the authors released a large-scale bimanual manipulation dataset comprising 3,255 episodes and approximately 39.7 hours (recorded at 30 Hz).

The dataset covers three tasks:
- Orange placement
- Water pouring
- Towel folding

The dataset includes fully synchronized left and right wrist videos, relative TCP poses, gripper opening states, and natural language task instructions. All data is formatted to the standard LeRobot specification, allowing it to be directly plugged into dataloaders for future frame prediction and Flow Matching training.

sections.heading: Strengths of UMI-Live and currently identified limitations
sections.summary: While achieving easy in-the-wild collection and high throughput, the paper candidly discusses operational constraints and future validation points, including device weight and LiDAR SLAM environment dependency.
sections.details:
Although UMI-Live frees data collection from physical robots and external tracking rigs, several limitations remain:

- **Device Weight**: Consolidating sensors, a Raspberry Pi, and a battery onto each hand results in a weight of 1.42 kg per gripper, placing physical strain on human operators during long collection sessions.
- **Reliance on LiDAR SLAM**: In geometrically featureless, flat environments or during abrupt accelerations, pose estimation accuracy from LiDAR and IMU risks degrading.
- **Calibration**: While per-environment calibration is unnecessary, initial calibration of camera intrinsics and finger opening width is required once after assembling the hardware.
- **Scope of Empirical Comparisons**: The real-robot evaluation was conducted on a single task with a single random seed, and ablation experiments testing "UMI data only" versus "teleoperation data only" were not performed, requiring further studies to fully isolate the individual contribution of each data source.

sections.heading: Summary: an open platform connecting handheld devices to real-robot deployment
sections.summary: UMI-Live provides a reproducible platform combining hardware design, automated software, a large dataset, and real-robot inference systems, powerfully accelerating the scaling of robot learning.
sections.details:
In this work, the authors proposed "UMI-Live," a completely self-contained system for collecting bimanual demonstration data effortlessly in the wild. A single button press coordinates recording with an asynchronous pipeline, automating everything through dataset generation.

The released ~40-hour dataset and high success rates on a physical robot with $\pi_{0.5}$ and MolmoAct2 demonstrate the practical utility of handheld collection data. With CAD files, bills of materials, setup guides, and training and inference code all open-sourced, the foundation is laid for anyone to reproduce the system and leverage it for their own robotics research.

sections.heading: Appendix: bills of materials and structures open for anyone to build
sections.summary: To allow anyone to replicate UMI-Live, comprehensive details on 3D printed parts, off-the-shelf sensors, and fasteners are fully disclosed.
sections.details:
The appendix provides detailed hardware specifications to ensure the reproducibility of UMI-Live.

All constituent components are cataloged, including the LiDAR, ultra-wide USB camera, Raspberry Pi 5, small LCD, swappable battery, DC-DC converter, linear guide rails, sector gears, and various fasteners (bolts, nuts, and bearings). 3D printed components can be fabricated using standard FDM printers with PLA+ and TPU, intentionally designed so that researchers can build the system in-house without specialized industrial machining equipment.

captions.F8: All components required to assemble a single UMI-Live gripper, organized including LiDAR, camera, Raspberry Pi, linear guides, gears, battery, and 3D printed parts.

takeaways: Completely eliminated external trackers and stationary cameras by consolidating LiDAR, IMU, camera, and compute onto the hand, enabling bimanual demonstration collection anywhere.
Achieved an exceptional workflow with zero collection downtime or manual post-processing by running parallel SLAM and annotation asynchronously on a server during data collection.

Demonstrated that state-of-the-art VLA models can achieve high success rates (up to 100%) even when over 90% of the training data comes from handheld devices in different rooms and lighting, mixed with just a small amount of target robot data.
Extremely low barrier to entry thanks to fully open-sourced hardware CAD, assembly guides, teleoperation software, training/inference code, and an approximately 40-hour dataset.
limitations: The 1.42 kg per-hand weight can be physically demanding and cause fatigue for human operators during extended continuous collection sessions.
LiDAR SLAM tracking accuracy risks degrading in geometrically flat spaces lacking distinctive structural features or during rapid hand movements.
The real-robot evaluation lacks direct comparative ablation experiments against "UMI data only" or "teleoperation data only," leaving the standalone contribution of each data source unseparated.
